The opening calculation used 28 anchor moments, but its endpoint comparison used only six tilted moments. I’ll give the direct calculation access to all 28. That will distinguish any gain in endpoint accuracy from a proof that the same gap widens throughout the interval.

On \([999,1000]\), the calculation certifies that the physical gap widens backward while the mean-normalized gap moves in the opposite direction. The transported endpoint width fell to \(2.55\times10^{-10}\); direct evaluation of the same 28 moments reached \(4.76\times10^{-45}\). I’ll now test whether the signed result survives on one overlapping earlier interval using the same anchor.

I want to emphasize the importance of placing any numerical results into the broader analytical context, the goal is to achieve something that generalizes to arbitrary heights and can propagate to times that are relevant for progress towards improving bounds on the De Bruijn Newman constant or something similar, and numerical checks tend to have less promise for those types of goals. Therefore they should always be pursued within the context of the broader goals, as checks, and not pursued for their own sake

I’ll make the arbitrary-height question the main conclusion. The first-pair calculation can check the cancellation, but it cannot establish how the method behaves at large height or near the Newman bound. I’ll examine whether the phase chart itself can survive in that regime and what analytical estimate would be needed there.
Please also modify the research overview, plan and progress files to align with that motivation, if they are not currently alighed

I’ll revise the overview, plan, and progress register so that each future computation has a stated analytical question and a decision it can change. I’ll also put the scope of the first-pair result alongside the arbitrary-height analysis in all three files.

I found a stronger limitation than a loss of numerical precision. Throughout the Newman-relevant time range, the sine part of this particular half-line transform is positive at every positive height. Any two positive real zeros therefore have the same phase, so the increasing phase chart used at \(t=1000\) cannot span them. I’ll record the proof and use the physical field directly for the low-time comparison.

**The main result is an all-height obstruction.** For every \(0\le t\le 1/2\), the half-line transform used in the opening manuscript has positive imaginary part at every positive height. Every positive real zero of the physical field therefore has the same phase, \(\pi/2\), and the phase current takes both signs between any two such zeros. This rules out using that increasing phase chart to propagate adjacent zeros into the Newman-relevant regime. The individual velocity formula \(H_{xx}/H_x\) still holds at simple zeros. [Proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/04_EZ_HALF_LINE_PHASE_OBSTRUCTION_20261120.md) · [Internal assessment](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/reviews/02_EZ_ANALYTICAL_SCOPE_AND_REPLAY_20261120.md)

Working directly with the physical field gives a positive result and identifies the remaining difficulty. A specialization of Polymath’s estimates proves \(\lvert H_t/\mathcal B_t\rvert>3/4\) throughout \(1/5\le y\le1\), uniformly for \(\tau\le t\le1/2\) and \(x\ge4\pi e^{32/\tau}\). At \(t=1/10\), that sufficient height is \(4\pi e^{320}\). On the lower edge of the strip, from \(x=14000\) through \(6.1\times10^{12}\), charging terms 2 through 16 separately already costs more than the entire leading term. Tightening the remaining error bounds alone cannot close that gap. The finite-height region and the intermediate-time barrier remain open, so this work gives no improved bound on \(\Lambda\). [Derivation and scope](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/05_EZ_EXPLICIT_POSITIVE_TIME_STRIP_TAIL_20261120.md) · [Polymath’s criterion](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S1)

The finite calculation answered its narrower question. The first gap widens backward throughout \([984,1000]\), while the gap multiplied by the source mean contracts. Direct evaluation using the same 28 moments gives a much narrower endpoint interval. Both certificates reproduced byte for byte. [Finite research note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/03_EZ_JOINED_PATH_20261120.md)

**Recommended continuation:** test whether transporting the *signed* error of the physical field across time preserves enough cancellation to lower the height at which a uniform estimate begins. Compare it with direct evaluation using identical source information. I think I'm a bit confused here. What half line transform are you referring to, and increasing phase chart? I thought that this investigation was building on 05_arithmetic_gap_continuation, which itself has an infinite hierarchy of moments M that depend on the separations between exterior zeros and a fixed pair, and M itself is indexed by which pair it is looking at. That does not seem to track with what you are describing. Am I missing something?
I’ll check the parent’s definitions and the branch’s derivation side by side so I can show exactly where the pair index enters and what the phase argument establishes.

You have the parent investigation right. It fixes a pair of zeros and asks how the exterior zeros drive that pair’s separation. My previous answer skipped the connection to that hierarchy and then recommended a separate strip problem. That made an auxiliary method sound like the main line of research.

For a pair \(x_n,x_{n+1}\), write \(g_n=x_{n+1}-x_n\) and \(D_n=g_n^2/4\). The parent’s exterior moments are
\[
S_{n,p}=\sum_{\rho\ \mathrm{exterior}}
\frac{1}{[(\rho-x_n)(\rho-x_{n+1})]^p},
\qquad M_n=S_{n,1}.
\]
There are two indices here. The pair index \(n\) determines which two zeros are excluded and where every separation is measured. The order \(p\) runs through the hierarchy for that pair. The first two evolution laws show why the higher moments matter:
\[
\dot D_n=2-4D_nM_n,\qquad
\dot M_n=2M_n^2-12S_{n,2}-16D_nS_{n,3}.
\]
[Parent pair equations](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/manuscript/sections/02_pair_chain.tex) · [Exterior moment hierarchy](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/manuscript/sections/03_hierarchy.tex)

The **half-line transform** was a device explored in the child investigation. The physical field \(H(t,x)\) is a cosine integral over \(u\geq 0\). The child replaces the cosine by \(e^{ixu}\) to form
\[
B_+(t,x)=\int_0^\infty e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)e^{ixu}\,du,
\qquad H(t,x)=\Re B_+(t,x)
\]
for real \(x\). An **increasing phase chart** is an interval of \(x\) on which \(B_+\) stays nonzero and its angle increases. On such an interval, successive crossings of the imaginary axis locate successive zeros of \(H\). The moments in the numerical check were moments of the integration variable \(u\). They measure a different quantity from the exterior-zero separations in \(S_{n,p}\). [Child investigation’s construction](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/manuscript/main.tex)

The link is the **velocity of the chosen gap**. The phase construction tried to estimate \(\dot g_n/g_n\) from the velocities of its two endpoints. The parent’s first equation then gives exactly
\[
M_n=\frac{1}{2D_n}-\frac12\frac{\dot g_n}{g_n}.
\]
So the phase method was one proposed way to estimate \(M_n\). The obstruction I reported limits that particular method. It leaves the exterior hierarchy and its evolution equations intact. [Derivation of the link](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/manuscript/current.tex)

I would revise my continuation guidance accordingly. The direct question is whether the exterior zero geometry gives a bound on \(12S_{n,2}+16D_nS_{n,3}\) strong enough to propagate control of \(M_n\), and hence \(D_n\), over a stated time interval **uniformly in the pair height**. The first-pair calculation did not establish such a bound. The strip problem I suggested is a separate direction and should have been presented that way.

Some comments:

- The hierarchy on S\_{n,p} was generalized to S\_{n,p,q}, which depends on \rho-c\pm \sqrt{D}. This seemed to be a more promising hierarchy, so I think the investigation should focus on that generalized hierarchy, which is closed under time derivatives. 
- It looks like to get the equation for M_n you inverted the equation for the gap time derivative. I think the equation for the gap time derivative is the more useful equation, because M can be estimated from precise knowledge of the zero locations, which is exactly what this investigation is trying to improve. It seems you have the reasoning backward here.
- I don't see any mention of the explicit formulas that were derived in the initial brainstorm note for this idea, /papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120 (this should actually be moved into a brainstorm directly within  05_arithmetic_gap_continuation, it was a mistake to put it in the 01_jacobi_integer_hierarchy investigation). It seems that the investigation has drifted fairly far from the initial motivation. I'd like to understand what happened.



It seems that we need to repair whatever broken link there is between the initial motivation for this sub-investigation and the current research targets, or I need to understand better how they are connected.

I’ll trace the original brainstorm through the parent hierarchy and the child’s research plan, then repair the files where the target changed. I’ll also move the brainstorm to the parent investigation and update its references.

I found where the target changed. The opening manuscript retained the explicit zero formulas, but its first research decision chose to estimate gap velocity directly. After that method failed at lower times, the plan switched to strip nonvanishing. I’m restoring the missing step from zero locations to the mixed moments, including a bound for the contribution of zeros beyond the explicit window.

The exterior calculation now recovers the sign of backward gap widening directly from the zero positions. The equally spaced approximation cancels in the gap equation. The first surviving term comes from the theta source variance, which accounts for zeros beyond the explicitly located ones. The proof covers a growing family of pairs at large time. The remaining question is how to propagate that information from one anchor to earlier times.

You identified a real change of direction. The founding question was to **use explicit zero locations to estimate the exterior moments, then use those moments to predict gap motion**. My previous recommendation reversed that reasoning.

The opening manuscript retained the brainstorm’s formula \(x_k(T)=Y((k-\tfrac12)\pi)/\mathbb E_T U\), including the convergent expansion for \(Y\). The first research decision, however, chose to estimate velocity directly from a phase current and then recover \(M_n\) from that velocity. When the phase method failed at lower times, I redirected the research toward strip nonvanishing. Neither decision established a limitation of the generalized hierarchy. I moved [the founding brainstorm](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/brainstorm/notes/08_SUMMING_THE_LARGE_TIME_ZERO_LOOP_20261120.md) to the parent investigation, preserved its formulas, and documented [where the two decisions occurred](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/07_EZ_ZERO_FORMULAS_AND_MIXED_HIERARCHY_CONTINUATION_20261120.md).

**The repaired calculation uses the hierarchy in the intended direction.** For each marked pair, the explicit formulas locate its endpoints and a growing set of exterior zeros. At a known all-real upper time, the even product accounts for every remaining zero through reciprocal power sums obtained from the theta source. Together these give an estimate for each fixed mixed moment \(S_{n,p,q}\), including \(M_n=S_{n,1,1}\). We then insert \(M_n\) into the gap equation \(D_n'=2-g_n^2M_n\). [Mixed-moment derivation](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/08_EZ_LOCALIZATION_TO_MIXED_MOMENTS_20261120.md)

This recovers a signed result. Exact lattice spacing would give \(g_n^2M_n=2\), so deciding whether the gap widens requires resolving the first correction. The complete exterior contributes a term from the theta source variance, giving
\[
\ell_T^2\bigl(g_n^2M_n-2\bigr)\longrightarrow\pi^2
\quad\text{for }n+1=o(\sqrt{\ell_T}),\qquad T\to\infty,
\]
where \(\ell_T=\mathbb E_T U\sqrt{\kappa_T}\) is the large-time scale from the brainstorm. Thus these gaps widen backward. The earlier phase proof covers a wider large-time range. What this derivation adds is an explanation of the sign **from the zero geometry and the complete exterior**, including the contribution lost by dropping the distant zeros. [Signed estimate and proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/notes/09_EZ_COMPLETE_ANCHOR_FROM_ZERO_FORMULAS_20261120.md:61) · [Internal assessment](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/03_explicit_zero_gap_transport/reviews/04_EZ_MIXED_MOMENT_ANCHOR_ASSESSMENT_20261120.md)

**The next question is propagation from one upper time.** The present proof estimates the exterior afresh at every sufficiently large time. The full mixed hierarchy is closed under differentiation, but successive derivatives involve higher orders. The revised plan targets their combined contribution to the time error in \(2-g_n^2M_n\), measured against the initial squared half-gap on every partial descent. That is the missing estimate for reaching earlier times. Arbitrary-height coverage at a fixed Newman-relevant time and an improved bound on \(\Lambda\) remain open. Excellent, can you create a new research overview, plan and progress file to reflec these goals? I think it will be easier to start from scratch than to modify the existing ones. Follow the guidance in INVESTIGATION_SETUP_WORKFLOW, making the research program focus primarily on analytical frameworks that can lead to simplifications which could ideally lead to improved control over the gaps, moments or improved bounds on the De Bruijn Newman constant. I think the research should start by understanding the explicit formulas for the zeros better, where they are valid, and improving them if possible, before focusing on the dynamics. It will be good to also compare these to the state of the art results in the polymath paper [https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12438](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12438) and the more recent paper [https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09765,](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09765,) to see if there is an advantage from the formulas here. The goal is to have as much of the exact locations of the zeros in our formulas at a given large time so that we can propagate them backwards in time analytically, ideally leading to improvements in modeling the gap spacing, to the point where it could improve bounds on \Lambda, etc.\

I’ll start a fresh set of planning files in the existing investigation. I’ll read the setup workflow and both papers, then use their actual time ranges, height ranges, and error estimates to frame the first research question about the explicit zero formulas.

The papers give two different benchmarks. Polymath gives a labelled location error at high height for \(0<t\leq 1/2\). Platt–Trudgian gives a finite-height count at \(t=0\) and the bound \(\Lambda\leq 0.2\). I’ve identified a common-time test at \(t=1/2\) for the repository’s exact product formula, so the plan can compare location accuracy without extrapolating the large-time expansion.

The program begins with **how many consecutive zeros can be located at one specified large time, and with what error relative to their spacing**. It compares the counted contour formula, the inverse in odd cumulants and its closed cubic approximation, and the full-product formula that recovers each fixed zero from even source moments. The first candidate improvement is to bound the *difference* between the errors at adjacent zeros. A shared error can cancel in the gap even when it limits the accuracy of either position alone.

The plan identifies a concrete comparison at \(t=1/2\), where both full-product recovery and Polymath’s high-zero location theorem apply. This makes it possible to test whether the product formula offers a genuine advantage at matched labels. Platt–Trudgian supplies the finite-height count at \(t=0\) and the published benchmark \(\Lambda\leq 0.2\). [Polymath, §9](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438v2#S9) · [Platt–Trudgian, Corollary 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2004.09765v1#page=5)

**The first research task is AGC-EZ-B07.** It maps where each formula is valid and selects one analytical improvement to prove. Backward transport through the mixed hierarchy follows once the position estimates establish which zeros are located, how accurately their separations are known, and how much the remaining exterior can contribute.
